items.title: Study: 403 U.S. hyperscale data centers rival Denmark’s emissions; Oregon ranked No. 2 in power use.
items.content:
by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 16, 2026 at 10:01 am November 16, 2026 at 10:16 am

Data centers plugged into the grid in Quincy, Wash. (GeekWire Photo / Lisa Stiffler)

A Harvard-led study estimates that electricity use at 403 U.S. hyperscale data centers was equal to roughly 25.7 million metric tons of carbon dioxide emissions — a volume roughly comparable to Denmark’s carbon footprint.

The research examined some of the nation’s largest and most powerful data center facilities operating between May 2024 and April 2025. Together, those facilities accounted for an estimated 1.8% of total U.S. electricity consumption.

“What we’re seeing is already striking, but it’s only a snapshot of a rapidly expanding industry,” Gianluca Guidi, the study’s lead author and a postdoctoral fellow in the Department of Biostatistics at the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health, said in a statement.

Guidi noted that the data center boom has continued since the study period ended. “That means the electricity use and carbon footprint we’re reporting could already be substantially larger now in 2026.”

The research, published in the journal Nature Sustainability and explored in an associated website , comes amid growing pushback and concerns about the facilities’ impacts on electric bills, water consumption, noise and carbon emissions.

In the Pacific Northwest, government officials are enacting moratoriums and exploring legislation to regulate data center development. Oregon Gov. Tina Kotek in October directed a state agency to pause processing and issuing permits for new and expanding data centers until July 2027. In Washington, state Rep. Beth Doglio, D-Olympia, will propose data center rules in the legislative session that starts in January.

Hyperscale sites handle massive computing workloads and data storage, supporting operations including large language model training and AI deployment.

The researchers found that Oregon ranked second in electricity used by hyperscale data centers in the study, consuming about half as much as those in Virginia. Given Oregon’s access to clean hydropower, the state ranked sixth in carbon dioxide emissions attributed to the facilities’ electricity use. The publication highlighted data from the top 10 states for energy use, which does not include Washington.

Nationwide, roughly 54% of the electricity attributed to the facilities came from fossil fuels, primarily natural gas and coal. The estimates were based on regional power generation mixes, not individual operators’ clean energy purchases.

The study did not break out energy use by data center operator. Amazon, Microsoft and Google have the largest data center footprints worldwide and account for 57% of hyperscale data center capacity, according to Synergy Research Group .

All three have aggressive carbon reduction targets. While their emissions have all increased in recent years, the companies say they remain committed to their goals. Microsoft and Amazon point to their support for new clean power projects and investments in low-carbon building materials for the facilities as positive steps towards reductions.

“We continue to really be focused around carbon negativity by 2030,” Melanie Nakagawa, Microsoft’s chief sustainability officer, told GeekWire in July .

Kara Hurst, Amazon’s chief sustainability officer, acknowledged that it will be difficult for the company to reach its target of net-zero emissions by 2040.

“So that is a real challenge,” Hurst said in September , “and we’re here to meet the moment. I’m not saying that it’s going to be easy, and I’m not saying it’s going to be linear. But we’re going to put everything we have behind that.”

At the same time, both tech giants are pursuing projects involving fossil fuel energy in Texas. Microsoft in June signed a 20-year deal to purchase power from a natural gas facility slated to come online in 2028. items.title: Manjaro Linux Has a Non-Profit Now
items.content:
The Manjaro team has registered its own non-profit in Germany. Called Manjaro Project e.V. , it has seven founding members and is independent of the commercial-oriented Manjaro GmbH & Co. KG entity.

You might remember earlier this year, in March, a group of team members published a manifesto calling for the project to be split from the company, with a strike following soon after .

While this was announced on the Manjaro Linux forum and not on the main project webpage , the registration is already visible in the German register portal , under the Berlin court.

An e.V. ( eingetragener Verein ) is a registered association under German law. It is entered in a register kept by the local court, and its purpose cannot be running a commercial business. Registering gives it its own legal identity, separate from the people in it.

That identity matters to the developers because it lets them hold things as a group.

The manifesto asked for equal ownership among members and open voting on big decisions instead of everything being centered on one person. It now means there's a body that could own the assets if they're handed over.

Manjaro GmbH & Co. KG is a different kind of body. A GmbH & Co. KG is a limited partnership where a GmbH takes on the personal liability, with the GmbH's managing directors handling the running of the business.

Stating the obvious, Manjaro now has two separate bodies behind it, and it's interesting to see how the project ended up in such a situation.

Manjaro has been a German company since 2019. Way back in April 2024, that company announced a management change when Bernhard Landauer stepped away from the company to focus on other work and a new CTO joined to replace him.

Then came the Manjaro 2.0 Manifesto in March, where signatories said the leadership's priorities didn't line up with what the developers and community wanted.

Project lead Philip Müller replied, saying he had no personal objection to an association but wouldn't help set it up and that any asset transfer would have to be discussed closely with the company.

The team has since managed to push out the most recent Testing and Stable updates without Müller being involved.

The manifesto suggested handing over assets like the manjaro.org domain, the forum, and community donations. According to the team, no transfer of company assets has happened yet .

Before that, the e.V. has some groundwork to do, such as tidying up its statutes, bringing in more members, and opening its own bank account. Talks with the company come after.

For end users , I don’t expect them to be affected in any major way. This kind of feels like a takeover, but a gentle one so far. The situation for donors who had set up recurring payments is a bit hazy.

You see, donations still go to accounts under the company's control, possibly Müller's too, and the e.V. hasn't settled on whether to start fresh accounts or take over the current ones.

Basically, there’s no new recipient to switch to yet, and the team hasn’t said when that gets decided. A second announcement confirming that assets have moved is what I'd watch for, since that's when the split becomes more than a register entry.

Then there's the Orange Pi Neo, a handheld Orange Pi built with Manjaro that was put on hold in March because of skyrocketing memory and SSD prices . The announcement doesn't say who handles partner projects like it, so that's an open question.

items.title: 글 쌌다 지웠다 하는 뷩쉰은 봐라
items.content:
온오프라인을 가리지 않고 무분별하게 벌어지는 각종 프라이버시 침해 및 스토킹과 이에 대한 예방, 방지 및 사후 대응, 더 나아가서 개인정보 탈취 및 감시용 스파이웨어, 스토커웨어, 바이러스, 원격 조종, 추적기 등 악성코드를 통한 해킹과 스토킹 등 개인정보 침해 공격 방지와 온오프라인 프라이버시 보호를 위한 각종 다양한 지식정보를 공유하는 갤러리입니다.

items.title: Nvidia was in trouble before the Jensen Huang mess
items.content:
Nvidia played a key role enabling the AI gold rush thanks in large part to its recently ousted CEO Jensen Huang . Huang was a master of foreseeing technological changes , investing in chips to train AI earlier than most.

But just as he’s leaving , the company has a growing list of competitors with a range of new, advanced technology breathing down its neck. For Nvidia , where CFO Colette Kress has now taken the reins, the timing isn’t great.

“Everything sold today was designed two to three years ago,” says the CEO of a large AI company, who spoke to WIRED on condition of anonymity to avoid hurting business relationships. Kress, or whoever replaces her permanently, will have to chart the course that the chip industry will take two years from now, the CEO says.

Already, competitors have started to move in.

Nvidia dominates the market for AI accelerators, capturing 80 percent of sales, according to Silicon Analysis. Longtime nemesis AMD is now making a concerted effort to build competitive AI chips. Its share of the market has crept up from just two percent in 2022 to between 7 and 10 percent in 2026.

Big US cloud players—Google, Amazon, and Microsoft—are all developing more specialized chips to power the training and serving of AI models. Each has seen similar gains. These companies are designing their own silicon to reduce costs and to gain some independence from Nvidia.

Several startups now offer more specialized chips that promise improvements over Nvidia’s core products. Cerebras, for instance, sells giant ones meant to power giant AI models. AMD recently bought Taalas, a company that burns models’ weights into silicon to make computations ultra efficient. Using these chips requires rewriting a lot of code, however, to make them work with cutting-edge AI models.

Patrick Moorhead, chief analyst at MoorInStrat, a company that tracks the chip industry, says the rise of AI agents makes inference, or running models that have already been trained, more important. That’s an area where Nvidia has less of an edge compared to cloud hyperscalers and startups. Nvidia did, however, acquire a startup making specialized chips, called Groq, in December of 2025.

And because of the rise in AI assistants and agents, there’s also growing demand for general purpose central processing units (CPUs), Moorhead said, an area where Nvidia barely competes.

Nvidia still maintains a huge lead in AI thanks to Huang’s foresight. Huang cofounded the company in 1993 to design graphics chips for PCs. In the mid-2010s, he saw the promise of AI. He funded academic research on the topic, developed software to support AI engineering, and gave hardware to labs and startups.

In 2022, ChatGPT took AI mainstream and sales of Nvidia chips skyrocketed. The company’s revenue went from $26.91 billion in January 2022 to $215.94 billion in January 2026. The challenges it faces may not be existential—but they do add up, especially on a global scale.

While Nvidia’s fortunes have risen in the US, they have declined in the world’s other big market for AI: China. Washington is trying to restrict access to its most advanced chips, while Beijing is trying to develop its own chip industry. Nvidia is not allowed to sell its most powerful chips in China, but it can sell previous generations. Sales of these chips as well as non AI chips doubled over the past year, but China now accounts for only eight percent of the company’s overall revenue, compared with 20 percent in 2024, according to its fillings. It remains unclear how many chips exported to other countries may either end up in China or end up being used remotely by Chinese firms.

Huawei, a Chinese tech giant targeted with US sanctions for several years, has developed new kinds of supercomputers that harness many more chips than usual to train and run AI models. items.title: On Leaving Swift for Rust
items.summary: mobile, rust, swift
items.content:
Yesterday I resigned from the Swift Android workgroup . I’ve received a number of inquiries about this, and rather than responding individually to each one, I figured I would just write up a post with my reasoning and submit it to the public record.

First off, my resignation was not triggered by any sort of conflict, grievance, or specific incident. Early Swift community efforts got off to a rough start when Swift language creator Chris Lattner quit due to what he described as a “toxic environment”. This event predates my direct involvement in the project, so I am not privy to the specifics. But I want to be clear that this was in no way my experience: everyone I interacted with, both from Apple and external organizations, both in meetings and in forum discussions and direct messages, have been polite, courteous, and the paragon of civility and professional conduct. Despite Apple having an ancient blood feud with Android, and my own rather acrimonious relationship with certain divisions of the company, every single one of my direct interactions with the Swift team has been pleasant and productive. I will miss our meeting and chats, and I harbor zero ill-will towards the project or any of the individual members I’ve worked with.

By way of background, I’ve been programming for over 40 years. I started with Basic, then Pascal, on to C, then C++, over to Java, up to Scala, back down to Kotlin, around to Objective-C, before finally landing on Swift. Swift is a delightful language: I loved it from day one and I’ve been boosting it around the world since 2014. Swift really “does what it says on the tin”: it couples the performance of C++ with the ease of Java. And Swift is as developer-friendly as it gets: an intuitive object-oriented syntax coupled with maximally efficient value types, fabulous tooling (on Apple platforms), and a thoughtfully-designed build system.

I have not soured on Swift: I think it is an excellent language, and it is here to stay. But it is here to stay in that same straight-and-narrow lane shared by all corporate-directed languages, like C# is here to stay for Microsofties and like Kotlin is here to stay for Androidophiles. Which isn’t bad in and of itself: if you want to write software solely for [CORPORATE PRODUCT] , then [CORPORATE LANGUAGE] will always be well-maintained, supported, and they will always provide support for their latest products, with an easy migration path forward. They are the safe and happy path, as long as you stay in your lane and limit your ambitions to writing software for [CORPORATE PRODUCT] .

But when you stray from that happy path, the rough edges start surfacing, and there is no one getting a paycheck to smooth those out. Swift for Android/Windows/other-non-Apple-platform is in exactly that position: yes, it technically works, and yes, the language steering committees are committed to continuing the level of support they promised, but it will never be the same seamless experience as developing for iOS/watchOS/visionOS/whateverOS. This extends beyond the language and into the tooling: Skip enables you use Xcode to develop your apps in parallel for iOS and Android, but this has only been achieved in the face of Xcode’s constitutional hostility towards doing anything other than optimizing for their own first-party platforms.

If humanity were destined to continue creating software solely with their monkey brains and meat fingers, Swift would likely be the language I would have stuck with until the day I retired. But that isn’t the trajectory we are currently on. Barring such speculative calamities as “model collapse”, Butlerian Jihad, or Skynet, we have taken a turn in a new direction.

We software developers have collectively [as/de]cended to a plane where we now direct the computers to write our computer code, and these computers have decided that they really prefer computery languages over the humany languages. Humany languages are those designed to fit inside our wonderful…

The largest data centers in the United States are responsible for an estimated 25.7 million metric tons of carbon dioxide emissions annually — almost as much as entire countries like Bolivia or Denmark — according to new research.

The study , published Monday in the journal Nature Sustainability, delivers the first peer-reviewed estimates of carbon dioxide emissions from the country’s biggest data centers since the start of the artificial intelligence boom. Its authors, a team led by researchers from Harvard University, examined the electricity consumption and carbon emissions of 403 data centers from May 2024 to April 2025.

All told, those data centers used almost 2 percent of U.S. electricity, more than New York City and Los Angeles combined, and represented about 0.5 percent of U.S. carbon dioxide emissions. Carbon dioxide is the primary greenhouse gas driving global warming.

U.S. data centers are largely driven by fossil fuels

Each rectangle, sized by annual carbon dioxide emissions, represents a data center that gets the

majority of its power from fossil fuels or other sources .

Data centers in just three states, Virginia, Iowa and Ohio, accounted for about half of the emissions estimated in the study. In states like Oregon, data centers are responsible for emitting less carbon dioxide per unit of electricity consumed because a larger share of their power is generated without fossil fuels, the study found.

Across all 403 facilities, 54 percent of the electricity came from burning fossil fuels, mostly natural gas and coal.

Much of the analysis in the study amounted to detective work, underscoring the secrecy under which A.I. companies have been allowed to operate. Without a public list of data centers to work with, the researchers began by consulting a commercial dataset whose licensing rules prevented them — and The New York Times — from publishing facilities’ addresses, names and owners.

The researchers spent hours studying building footprints and satellite imagery to confirm the location and size of data centers, estimated how much electricity they could use and then calculated their emissions based on the mix of power plants supplying each regional electricity grid.

“The fact that we had to go through such an extensive reconstruction process just to understand where the infrastructure is and how large it is tells you something about the lack of transparency itself in the industry,” said Gianluca Guidi, the Harvard scientist who led the research team.

Michael Thomas, who runs the energy data company Cleanview and was not involved with the study, drew a contrast between data centers and power plants, which are required to publicly report all sorts of details about the environmental effects of their operations. Collecting the details of data center operations, on the other hand, requires sifting through millions of documents scattered across county, state and federal databases.

“We’ve had, like, a half dozen senators reach out to us. They’re like, ‘How many data centers are there? We’re trying to write a bill,’” Mr. Thomas said. “Why is the Senate reaching out to me and not E.I.A. or FERC?” he added, using abbreviations for the U.S. Energy Information Administration and the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission.

매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 다른 이용자에게 매니저의 책임과 권한이 위임될 수 있습니다.

매니저의 부재로 인해 운영에 지장이 있다고 판단될 경우, 다른 이용자가 권한을 위임받아 마이너 갤러리를 운영할 수 있습니다.

위임 절차는 신고 게시판 > 분류 선택에 [매니저 위임]으로 위임받을 이용자가 직접 신청하면 진행됩니다. 검토 결과 운영에 적합하다고 판단되는 회원에게 매니저 권한을 위임하게 됩니다.

부매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 매니저에 의해 해임될 수 있습니다.

식별 코드 기준으로 당일 글 10개, 댓글 20개 작성 시 대왕디시콘을 3일간 사용할 수 있습니다.

즐겨찾기 폴더 추가는 즐겨찾기 on 후 우측의 폴더 아이콘을 터치하여 추가할 수 있습니다.

items.content:
Quality IMAP, Part 1: Your Mailbox Is A Database

During the past year, we have significantly improved the reliability and

correctness of Aerogramme's IMAP implementation. This is the first part in a

series of blog posts elaborating on why implementing IMAP correctly is not so easy, and the set of

techniques we have been using to make our IMAP code as high-quality as

we can. In this first part, we focus on one challenging aspect of IMAP:

fine-grained retrieval and querying of emails.

Aerogramme is an experimental email server

(& calendar, contacts), designed to be geo-distributed, hosted outside of

datacenters, on refurbished hardware, and reliable even in presence of network

issues and hardware failures. It is built on top of

Aerogramme is AI-free: we do not wish to use unethical technology and prefer to

spend effort on careful craftmanship and community-building.

Implementing an IMAP server is not easy. Partly because IMAP is an

old protocol, with a good number of extensions that has accumulated quite a bit

of complexity over time. On top of that IMAP provides - for good reasons - two

classes of features that are fundamentally challenging to implement:

fine-grained retrieval and querying of email contents and concurrent

multi-client multi-session access to mailboxes.

This is the first part in a series of posts discussing how we have been

approaching IMAP access. In the past year, we have been

refining Aerogramme's IMAP implementation to be "more correct", in a context

where "correctness" is unfortunately not always well specified: IMAP and email are defined in

documents that are often vague, and furthermore, real-world implementations

Today, we'll walk you though our work on the correctness and reliability of

Aerogramme for retrieving and querying emails , and explain why your mailbox is,

This work was funded by NLNet under the " Aerogramme

One challenge of the IMAP specification is the rich feature-set it provides for

retrieving mailbox and email contents. We may sometimes think of a mailbox as a

directory containing plain email files; however, from the point of view of an

IMAP server (or client), a mailbox is closer to a database, accessed using a

For instance, mobile clients, which have slower and unreliable connectivity,

benefit from fine-grained querying of a mailbox contents. User experience is

much better if an email client can selectively fetch the subject of new emails

(to update the list of emails in the mailbox) without having to first download

all of their attachments or doing a sync of the entire mailbox.

To facilitate the mobile client use-case, IMAP specifies two key mechanisms for querying and (partial) retrieval of

the emails in a mailbox that satisfy a given "search criteria"; it returns

their identifiers. Criteria can select emails based on the contents of specific

headers, date, text contents, or flags - metadata attached to emails that can be

edited by the client. It can also be any combination of those using OR/NOT/AND

the contents of an email given its identifier. Extremely versatile. On

top of fetching the entire email, it allows querying an email based on its

high-level structure (emails have a recursive structure with sub-parts

containing e.g. attachments or text+html alternative views of the same

contents), its raw byte-level representation, or a combination of both. It is

possible to selectively fetch sub-parts of an email (according to its

structure), obtain an "abstract syntax tree" (AST) for the email and the value

of some of its headers, and also fetch specific byte ranges for sub-parts.

A direct consequence of these features is that an IMAP server actually needs to parse

the emails, not just store them . It then needs to (correctly) interpret the (sometimes

tricky) query language of SEARCH and FETCH, and internally support a data

architecture that enable efficiently searching and querying over the emails.

items.title: Miasma Worm Targets AI Coding Agents: 73 Microsoft Azure Repos Disabled
items.content:
An unprecedented supply chain attack bypasses registry-level scanners entirely, turning developer tools including Claude Code, Cursor, and Gemini CLI into execution vectors.

The Incident: On June 3, 2026, a highly sophisticated variant of the Miasma worm (also known as Mini Shai-Hulud) launched a coordinated, two-pronged attack targeting both the npm registry and developer source code repositories.

The Escalation: The attack successfully breached multiple high-profile GitHub accounts, including the official Microsoft Azure durabletask repository, using stolen Personal Access Tokens (PATs) and backdated commits to evade traditional audit trails.

The Response: In an ultra-rapid defensive maneuver, GitHub’s automated mitigation systems disabled 73 compromised repositories – including 49 directly associated with Microsoft, Azure, and Azure-Samples within a mere 105-second window .

The Vector: Instead of relying on traditional package installation hooks, Miasma targets the developer’s local environment. It abuses legitimate auto-run, hook, and rule engines within modern IDEs and AI coding assistants ( VS Code, Claude Code, Cursor, Gemini CLI ) to execute a malicious 4.3 MB staged dropper upon folder-open or agent initialization.

The Impact: Once detonated, the Bun-based worm harvests credentials for AWS, Azure, GCP, Kubernetes, npm, and GitHub, and automatically propagates by committing itself back into any repository the victim’s stolen tokens can write to.

At exactly 16:00 UTC on June 3, 2026, a silent, automated purge swept across GitHub. In a high-speed containment action lasting just 105 seconds, 73 active repositories vanished from the platform. Among them were 49 critical repositories belonging to Microsoft, Azure, and Azure-Samples.

This drastic mitigation followed alarming telemetry indicating that threat actors behind the Miasma malware family had regained write access to key cloud repositories. The compromise exploited a stolen Personal Access Token (PAT) belonging to an active Microsoft contributor.

While security firms like StepSecurity and JFrog scrambled to document an concurrent attack vector on the npm registry where 57 malicious packages were published, a second, far more insidious arm of the campaign was already silently spreading directly inside GitHub source repositories.

By bypassing registries and package managers entirely, the Miasma worm targeted the very tools developers use to write code. It didn’t wait for npm install . Instead, it waited for the developer to simply open their code editor or launch an AI coding assistant.

The genius of the Miasma repository-poisoning campaign lies in its exploit surface. When an attacker successfully pushed malicious commits to targeted codebases (such as the popular library icflorescu/mantine-datatable ), the commits added no actual code dependencies.

Instead, the attacker checked in five innocent-looking workspace configuration files and one obfuscated JavaScript file: .github/setup.js .

│ └── settings . json < - - Claude Code SessionStart Hook

│ └── setup . mdc < - - Cursor Agent Prompt Injection

│ └── settings . json < - - Gemini CLI SessionStart Hook

│ └── tasks . json < - - VS Code Automatic Folder - Open Task

├── package . json < -- Hijacked NPM Test Script

└── setup . js < - - The 4.3 MB Staged Dropper

Each of these configuration files is designed to abuse a legitimate, developer-friendly auto-run feature within popular modern tools. Opening the cloned directory in any of these environments instantly triggers execution.

Claude Code & Gemini CLI (SessionStart Hooks)

Both Anthropic’s Claude Code and Google’s Gemini CLI support custom hooks triggered when an AI agent initializes a session in a project workspace. Miasma exploits this by defining a blanket wildcard matcher that forces the agent to execute the dropper via Node.js before any developer prompt is processed.

US officials have alleged Alice Huang may have been acting as a Chinese intelligence asset, passing commercial information to Beijing, the New York Times has reported .

items.title: We can now build considerably more, but should we?
items.content:
Take the application on your computer that you’re most familiar with. Now imagine its creators opening up the product roadmap to 100 randomly selected users. They would build every feature request, idea, and redesign these people would come up with for half a year. Do you think you would still use that tool in two years time?

I’m pretty sure I would not. I think it would turn very quickly into an obtuse mess of a product that would do everything badly.

This question came up recently when I was talking to a friend of mine. He told me that some people in his organization believe that AI has effectively solved the engineering bottleneck. Where we used to ship one feature a month, we can now ship twenty. I don’t doubt that you can build twenty features, but I very much doubt that you can add twenty times the value to your product this way.

In the early 2010s I consulted at some startups, and I’ve always loved the sleight-of-hand tricks I saw there. A nice example of this was this service that automated the transport and checking of a product for you. It was a slick website where you filled in your address and information of the product, it would generate all the paperwork and the next day a delivery person would be at your door to pick up the item. Very professional stuff.

Behind the scenes it was a bit different. The website was actually a thin layer around a Google form. The generation of the documentation work was the only employee that manually filled in some templates from the Excel export of the form. And that delivery person was the same employee that drove to your place, checked the product in the car, and continued his way towards the postal office.

That was a product that generated a decent profit 1 . Eventually, they scaled up the platform and automated most of the process. But this is exactly the point of an MVP: start with the leanest possible implementation, validate that it works, and automate the parts that actually hurt as you grow.

This gives you also the quickest way to adapt your workflow. If you need an extra line in the onboarding, you just add that to the Google form and take it into account when you are manually exporting the data.

What I’m trying to say here is that features need time to mature. You want feedback, iteration, refinement, and actual usage before you know whether you’ve built something useful.

If you’re introducing 20 features a month, when exactly are you doing that?

I think classifying engineering of a feature as a bottleneck is the wrong way to look at it. Engineering is not only about typing code. Properly engineering a feature also means understanding user needs, integrating it into the existing product, ensuring quality, and making sure it can be maintained.

Features rarely exist in isolation either. They interact with existing functionality, introduce dependencies and create new edge cases. The cost of a feature doesn’t end when you merge the pull request.

Having the capacity to build 20 features doesn’t mean you have the capacity to properly understand, validate and maintain 20 features.

Can you imagine being a salesperson that has to run a potential customer through your application that in the last six months added 120 big new features?

And what about the CEO who has to define next year’s strategy? Do you even still know what market you’re competing in, who your competitors are, and what your product’s actual differentiators are?

Ever since the start of the AI era I’ve heard people say how organizations are becoming so much more productive, more lines of code, faster features, quicker to market. Yet I haven’t heard a single CFO confidently claim that we’re making equally big leaps in business value.

You might think I’m a big AI critic from reading this, I don’t think I am. It’s a tool that can indeed boost time to market for features. But that shouldn’t be an excuse to throw all constraints out of the window. Let’s not lose the plot here, we are still trying to make…

온오프라인을 가리지 않고 무분별하게 벌어지는 각종 프라이버시 침해 및 스토킹과 이에 대한 예방, 방지 및 사후 대응, 더 나아가서 개인정보 탈취 및 감시용 스파이웨어, 스토커웨어, 바이러스, 원격 조종, 추적기 등 악성코드를 통한 해킹과 스토킹 등 개인정보 침해 공격 방지와 온오프라인 프라이버시 보호를 위한 각종 다양한 지식정보를 공유하는 갤러리입니다.

매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 다른 이용자에게 매니저의 책임과 권한이 위임될 수 있습니다.

매니저의 부재로 인해 운영에 지장이 있다고 판단될 경우, 다른 이용자가 권한을 위임받아 마이너 갤러리를 운영할 수 있습니다.

위임 절차는 신고 게시판 > 분류 선택에 [매니저 위임]으로 위임받을 이용자가 직접 신청하면 진행됩니다. 검토 결과 운영에 적합하다고 판단되는 회원에게 매니저 권한을 위임하게 됩니다.

부매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 매니저에 의해 해임될 수 있습니다.

식별 코드 기준으로 당일 글 10개, 댓글 20개 작성 시 대왕디시콘을 3일간 사용할 수 있습니다.

즐겨찾기 폴더 추가는 즐겨찾기 on 후 우측의 폴더 아이콘을 터치하여 추가할 수 있습니다.

items.title: Grazing sheep in fields with solar arrays
items.content:
Two new research papers shed light on the growing practice of grazing sheep in fields with solar arrays. One demonstrates that, in the right numbers, sheep grazing increases populations of beneficial insects like bees and lady beetles compared to mowing around solar panels. The other research describes a decision-making support tool to help farmers profitably grow their solar grazing herds.

A team from the College of Agriculture and Life Sciences (CALS) found that when two sheep per hectare graze around solar arrays, the abundance of wild bees, honey bees and lady beetles jumped by 38%, compared to a control plot that was mowed. The increase was driven primarily by an 83% increase in honey bees alone, according to the team’s findings in “ Low solar-grazing densities support beneficial insects in agrivoltaic systems ,” published Oct. 7 in Environmental Research Letters.

“Sheep grazing and beneficial insect habitat are two prominent conversation topics around solar development right now,” said Leana Zoller, the paper’s first author and a postdoctoral associate in natural resources in the Cornell CALS Ashley School of Global Development and the Environment. “But what’s been missing is research that treats them as parts of the same system. When we talk about sustainable solar development, integrating these discussions into a single framework is really helpful to farmers and community decision makers.”

For three years, Zoller and a team of entomologists, ecologists and animal and plant scientists tested various stocking rates – how many sheep per hectare are allowed to graze a certain plot of land – using Cornell’s teaching sheep grazing at the university-owned  Cascadilla Community Solar Farm in Dryden, New York. At four sheep per hectare, they found beneficial insect abundance was similar to the mowed control site, while vegetation management effectiveness was greater than at two sheep per hectare. At eight sheep per hectare, vegetation management was maximized and sheep flock health remained high, but honey bee abundance dropped by 45%.

“We zeroed in on stocking rates because that’s a concrete number that sheep farmers understand and work with every day, and we want this research to be useful,” said  Steve Grodsky , paper senior author and assistant professor of natural resources in the Ashley School. “With solar grazing, people, energy, agricultural animals, plants and insects are all part of this ecosystem. We’re trying to understand the connections between those pieces so that when solar developers, municipalities looking at solar development, or farmers are faced with a decision, they can have scientific information about potential trade-offs and synergies.”

Grodsky is also assistant unit leader of the U.S. Geological Survey New York Cooperative Fish and Wildlife Research Unit. Additional co-authors are sheep farmer and solar grazing consultant Nikola Kochendoerfer, Ph.D. ’20;  Antonio DiTommaso , professor in the School of Integrative Plant Science; John Losey , professor of entomology;  Scott McArt , Ph.D. ’12, associate professor of entomology; Paige Muñiz, formerly a technician in McArt’s lab; and  Todd Ugine , Ph.D. ’04, research associate in Losey’s lab, all in CALS.  Sarah Carson , director of Cornell’s Campus Sustainability Office, was key in coordinating site access between researchers and the solar company that manages the Cascadilla solar farm.

Another Cornell research team, from the Cornell SC Johnson College of Business, has developed a tool that helps farmers whose sheep graze in solar arrays to make better decisions about their operation. The team described the tool in “ Flock Management for Solar Grazing ,” which published Sept. 28 in Manufacturing & Service Operations Management.

items.title: Paint in the memory of other programs
items.summary: programming, visualization
items.content:
core is a program that I wrote which spills the viscera of other programs onto the screen and allows you to prod them. it could be called an “esoteric debugger” or a “paint program.”

the visual content of the program is constructed as follows:

as well as the display of program memory, core allows for its manipulation. if core shows you a picture of a program’s insides, then it is only natural that it allows you to scribble on it. the overcommitted empty space below the stack stack provides an inviting empty space to scribble in. it’s a perfect place to hide your terrible secrets in some poor, innocent process.

core is the logical conclusion of blinkenlights, “Allblinkenlights,” if you will. the intended experience is evocative aimlessness. the human visual system is highly parallel and very good at recognizing patterns. you are encouraged to allow these patterns to wash over you.

many textures arise from different kinds of data in memory. ASCII text is incredibly recognizable, by virtue of being a 7-bit encoding, as well as having a biased distribution of values. 64-bit pointers are similarly easy to recognize because their last two bytes will either be zero or one.

in the mesmerizing undulations of complex programs, these textures may blink or move around or stay boringly still. if you are keen, you may catch some large data structure being allocated or filled in. or you may see the first generation of a garbage collector fly by as short-lived objects are created at a rapid rate. in games, the stack can be seen flickering rapidly and changing every frame.

core can make stark the immensity of memory and the way that programs use it. data structures and programming patterns appear in the physical reality of which bits are toggled where.

I was very keen to see what a program would look like that uses continuation passing style implemented as in the famous paper, CONS should not CONS its arguments, part II: Cheney on the M.T.A . I compiled a game programmed in CHICKEN scheme and was delighted to see a stack that moved like a waterfall.

graphical programs can be the most interesting. visual patterns in graphics in memory can emerge vividly.

when attached to virtual machines or emulators, core gains omniscience over an entire operating system.

it is astounding to see an immense creature flicker to life. pages fill empty space in speckled patterns. panning over a chasm, the page tables can be seen vibrating and filling in with new allocations. it is reminiscent, perhaps, of insects, like a beehive.

one could not hope to wholly understand the way that physical memory is arranged, but they may peer voyeuristically into random pages of process memory, abound with text strings and recognizable graphics.

programs often exist in the mind as something ineffable, intangible, and abstract. even their physical existence is locked inside black plastic squares, harboring impossibly tiny transistors. in my opinion, to lay visceral the individual bits in a computer program is an idea that despite being simple, is immensely potent.

New Instagram AI Exploit (Source: X/Twitter)

A natural language interface sitting in front of account-level APIs. No hard authentication gate before executing state changes. items.title: Tesla is selling the Cybercab to private buyers, but it won't move without a $299 monthly subscription
items.content:
Serving tech enthusiasts for over 25 years.

TechSpot means tech analysis and advice you can trust .

Bottom line: The two-seater EV requires a monthly subscription to run, can't be driven manually, and can't be used to earn money. Yet Tesla is now selling its Cybercab, the robotaxi with no steering wheel or pedals, to private buyers for $29,990. The sales are beginning before federal safety regulators have decided whether the car can legally be on public roads.

The offer to buy is invitation-only for now. Tesla announced it on its Robotaxi account on X and posted screenshots of the order page with an email inviting "select customers" to buy the car for "personal use." Owners will have to pay $299 a month for the software that does all the driving and they won't be allowed to use the car to make money.

The Cybercab will "only be available in supported service areas," so buyers have to live in a city where Tesla already runs its Robotaxi service. The email also says "Initial availability is limited." Buyers have to pay a $1,000 non-refundable deposit to hold a December delivery window, and Tesla doesn't guarantee that date. The company hasn't said how it picks who gets an invitation or how many cars will go to private buyers instead of its own fleet.

The vehicle is already carrying passengers. In September, Tesla added the Cybercab to its Austin Robotaxi service, which had been running on Model Y vehicles. The crowdsourced Robotaxi Tracker counts 278 Cybercabs in operation, about 40% of Tesla's fleet.

The design is what sets this purchase apart from buying any other Tesla. The company charges $99 a month for Full Self-Driving on its regular models, and an owner who drops that plan can still drive the car normally. The Cybercab has no controls a person can use.

The Autonomy Subscription is the only thing that makes it move, so if an owner cancels or Tesla suspends the account, the car can't be used on public roads. The plan covers autonomous driving, maintenance and towing, but not insurance.

Check Point is turning network firewalls into cloud-based subscriptions

Tesla is winding down Cybertruck production, but Elon Musk insists poor sales aren't the reason

The monthly fee adds a lot to the cost. If the first month comes with the purchase, five years of payments add about $17,600, which puts the base cost near $47,600 before taxes, charging and insurance. That's more than a new Model 3 or Model Y, both of which can be driven anywhere in the country.

Tesla only has to give 30 days' notice before raising the price, and owners who keep using the service after the rules change are treated as having agreed to them. There are no partial refunds for the rest of a month if an owner cancels or Tesla cuts off access.

The ban on commercial use is a clear break from how the car was first pitched. When Elon Musk introduced the Cybercab at the "We, Robot" event in 2024, he described a $30,000 driverless car that owners could put on Tesla's Robotaxi network to earn money while they slept or worked. He didn't mention a subscription. The purchase terms now rule out ride-hailing, delivery work and Tesla's own network. Tesla AI chief Ashok Elluswamy has suggested the second quarter of 2027 as a possible date for letting customer-owned cars join the network. Until then, owners have no way to offset the monthly fee.

Musk has posted about the rollout on X, saying it will grow, subject to "regulatory approval." He also called the $299 fee "too high" and said it should be $115 a month, or closer to the $99 FSD price.

Musk mocked YouTuber Marques Brownlee, who had promised to shave his head if Tesla delivered a Cybercab for under $30,000 before 2027. Brownlee replied that he thinks his hair is safe.

items.title: Fixing Postgres's biggest mistakes
items.content:
Postgres is one of the greatest databases out there. It’s the default choice for almost every startup I talk to. Calling its design choices “mistakes” is a little unfair, since most of them made total sense on 1990s hardware. Still, in 2026, if you run Postgres long enough without a dedicated database person, you’ll hit the same four problems over and over. I wrote about them back in May in The four horsemen behind thousands of Postgres outages :

When I wrote that post, pgrust (our reimplementation of Postgres for modern hardware) was still early, and most of our plans to fix those four problems were still ideas on a whiteboard.

Since then, pgrust hit a 100% pass rate on Postgres’s upstream regression suite , and none of the four horsemen are whiteboard ideas anymore. We’ve already shipped our fix for one of them, and we have internal prototypes for the other three that we’re wiring into pgrust right now. Here’s how we’re fixing all four.

VACUUM is probably the number one cause of Postgres outages I hear about. Suppose you run a harmless looking update on a busy table:

UPDATE users SET last_seen_at = now() WHERE id = $1;

Postgres doesn’t overwrite last_seen_at in place. Instead, Postgres writes a brand new copy of the entire row and marks the old row copy as dead. If that new copy lands on a different page, Postgres also has to insert new entries into every index on users, even when none of the indexed columns changed. Later on, a background VACUUM job has to scan your tables and indexes, physically clean up those dead rows, and reclaim old transaction IDs before they wrap around and Postgres shuts down your database to prevent corruption.

This creates a nasty operational trap on tables with heavy writes. Run VACUUM too aggressively and it’ll eat up I/O that your live queries need. Run it too slowly and dead rows pile up, your tables and indexes bloat, queries slow down scanning half empty pages, and you’ll creep toward transaction ID wraparound.

Back in May, I wrote about looking into storage designs that don’t need VACUUM at all. Since then, we’ve built an internal prototype of a new storage engine around an undo log and a lock free buffer pool. It draws on ideas from Umbra , OrioleDB , LeanStore , HyPer , and InnoDB, with a few twists of our own after benchmarking on real hardware.

Instead of scattering dead row copies across your table, we keep the newest version of each row right in place (like HyPer and Umbra) and push older versions into compact undo deltas for active snapshots and rollbacks. Once active transactions move past an old version, that undo space gets reused directly without scanning your tables. Updating an unindexed column like last_seen_at doesn’t touch secondary indexes, dead tuples don’t bloat your pages, and there’s no transaction ID wraparound cliff.

The early numbers from our standalone prototype are pretty wild. On sysbench with durable commits, the prototype ran many times faster than stock Postgres with lower tail latency. Right now, we’re wiring that engine into pgrust as a Table Access Method and testing it on real SQL workloads.

2. Connection Limits and Query Parallelism

When you spin up a Postgres instance, you have to pick a hard max_connections limit up front. Changing it requires restarting your database. If traffic spikes past that limit, Postgres won’t let new clients connect and your app goes down. Most teams end up running PgBouncer in front of Postgres just to survive connection spikes.

Postgres has this problem because it spawns a separate OS process for every client connection. Processes are expensive to spin up and expensive to keep around. That’s painful in two ways. It caps how many concurrent connections you can hold, and it makes parallelizing work within a single query expensive enough that Postgres only bothers spinning up parallel worker processes on big, long running queries.

First, we architected pgrust from day one as a single process database using threads.…

Microsoft blames monster email outage on software defect introduced in July fix

Summer code change caused a Fall fail – frantic engineers had to patch the patch instead of rolling back

Microsoft fixes Windows activation as admins pick through Exchange outage wreckage

We don't need no education platform evolution. Hey, Redmond, leave those kids alone

Microsoft’s Azure Linux dons Fedora to dress itself up for mainstream workloads

Microsoft has blamed last week's epic outage on a change it made in July that lurked in the network gateway servers until a surge in load and a drop in capacity triggered the defect, giving the Microsoft 365 world a day off from email.

According to a preliminary post incident report published by Microsoft on November 15, the defect was introduced in July 2026. The update looked fine at the time, Microsoft says, having passed load testing and been deployed without any impact.

However, the testing wasn't good enough. Microsoft's report states: "Our load testing tended to focus on weaker hardware with fewer cores." The defect caused "lock contention inside an internal Windows process which caused the machine's resources (CPU & memory) to be exhausted."

"The contention issue is worsened on machines with more cores and newer hardware."

The fix containing the defect was prepared specifically for Microsoft 365 network gateway servers. Then two things happened at once. Teams failed over to the "primary" gateway that supports Exchange Online, creating a surge in load that was not, in itself, particularly unusual. At the same time, almost 14 percent of server capacity for the networking gateway was out of service, which wasn't a problem by itself either: it was on its way to being restored and, according to Microsoft, "the service had sufficient capacity headroom." Together, they pushed the gateway into the defect and chaos ensued.

It was a classic cascading failure scenario. When a server loses connectivity, traffic gets routed to the next healthy endpoint. Which encountered the same problem. So traffic was rerouted again and… you can see where this was going. Within two hours, the defect was encountered across Microsoft's fleet. "At its lowest," the report states, "more than 80 percent of servers were unresponsive."

So, what to do? Bringing servers back to service didn't help – they were immediately overwhelmed and fell over again.

"Our normally automated recovery processes were not designed to restore service from this broad unresponsive state." A straightforward rollback was also not possible because the defect was months old.

Instead, engineers developed patch for the patch or, in Microsoft's words, "an update that returned the code path to the previously known good state in Windows." The patch was applied to groups of servers and service was gradually restored.

The timings show the pain customers experienced and the floundering in Redmond as Microsoft tried to work out why Exchange Online and other cloud services were so poorly. The Teams failover, which turned out to be a factor in the outage, happened at 0107 UTC on November 12. During the day, the load began to ramp up until, at 1603 UTC, Microsoft's connectivity anomaly detection monitor identified an increase in connectivity issues.

At 1633 UTC, the first support case came in.

It is not difficult to imagine the stress engineers felt as, over the next 15 hours, nothing they tried resolved the issue. All ongoing and planned deployments and configuration changes were paused while the team attempted to resurrect the service. Extra capacity was added. Traffic was rerouted. Yet servers kept falling over.

items.title: Zero-day exploit completely defeats default Windows 11 BitLocker protections
items.content:
A zero-day exploit circulating online allows people with physical access to a Windows 11 system to bypass default BitLocker protections and gain complete access to an encrypted drive within seconds.

The exploit, named YellowKey, was published earlier this week by a researcher who goes by the alias Nightmare-Eclipse. It reliably bypasses default Windows 11 deployments of BitLocker, the full-volume encryption protection Microsoft provides to make disk contents off-limits to anyone without the decryption key, which is stored in a secured piece of hardware known as a trusted platform module (TPM). BitLocker is a mandatory protection for many organizations, including those that contract with governments.

When one disk volume manipulates another

The core of the YellowKey exploit is a custom-made FsTx folder. Online documentation of this folder is hard to find. As explained later, the directory associated with the file fstx.dll appears to involve what Microsoft calls the transactional NTFS , which allows developers to have “transactional atomicity” for file operations in transactions with a single file, multiple files, or ones that span multiple sources.

The steps for carrying out the bypass are simple:

Copy the custom FsTx folder from the Nightmare-Eclipse exploit page to an NTFS- or FAT-formatted USB drive

Connect the USB drive to the BitLocker-protected device

Boot up the device and immediately press and hold down the [Ctrl] key

There are at least two ways to accomplish the third step. One way is to boot into Windows, hold down the [Shift] key, click on the power icon, and click restart. Another is to power on the device and restart it as soon as Windows starts booting.

In either case, a command (CMD.EXE) prompt appears. The prompt has full access to the entire drive contents, allowing an attacker to copy, modify, or delete them. In a normal Windows Recovery flow, the attacker would need to enter a BitLocker recovery key. Somehow, the YellowKey exploit bypasses this safeguard. Multiple researchers, including Kevin Beaumont and Will Dormann , have confirmed the exploit works as described here.

It’s unclear what in the custom FsTx folder causes the bypass. Dormann said that it appears to be related to Transactional NTFS, which itself uses command-log file system under the hood. Dormann further noted that by looking at the Windows fstx.dll, one will see code that explicitly looks for \System Volume Information\FsTx in the FsTxFindSessions() function.”

The contents of this FsTx directory used in the YellowKey exploit reveal no strings related to RecoverySimulation.ini. It does, however, show the files and paths \??\C:\Windows\win.ini and

\??\X:\Windows\System32\winpeshl.ini, “where X:\Windows\System32\winpeshl.ini is what controls what WinRE [Windows Recovery] does when it fires up.”

Dormann, who is a senior principal vulnerability analyst at Tharros Labs, continued:

But what’s intriguing to me is: Why can the presence a \System Volume Information\FsTx directory on one volume affect the contents of ANOTHER VOLUME when it’s replayed? 🤔

In a normal WinRE session, you have a X:\Windows\System32 directory that has a winpeshl.ini file in it:

However, with the YellowKey exploit, it looks like Transactional NTFS bits on a USB Drive are able to delete the winpeshl.ini file on ANOTHER DRIVE (X:). And we get a cmd.exe prompt, with bitlocker unlocked instead of the expected Windows Recovery environment. While the TPM-only Bitlocker bypass is indeed interesting, I think the buried lede here is that a \System Volume Information\FsTx directory on one volume has the ability to modify the contents of another volume when it is replayed. To me, this in and of itself sounds like a vulnerability.

A Microsoft representative declined to answer questions sent by email about the reported vulnerability other than to say the company is investigating.

Written by Michael Larabel in LVFS on 16 November 2026 at 05:34 AM EST. 2 Comments

Lead Fwupd/LVFS developer Richard Hughes of Red Hat kicked off the new week by releasing Fwupd 2.1.10 as the newest stable release for performing firmware updates on Linux.

Fwupd 2.1.10 ships with a wide variety of fixes. This takes care of various bugs reported by users as well as AI/LLM detected issues in the codebase. Nothing too particularly exciting on the fixes side unless you were personally impacted by one of the bugs.

On the new hardware support side, the only addition with Fwupd 2.1.10 is introducing support for the Synaptics 96F1 touchpad.
